architecture.mechanism: Hazard and operability study (HAZOP)-based identification of failure modes and influences of main components, followed by architecture optimization using redundant design to reduce failure frequency and unavailability.
architecture.intervention: Apply HAZOP to the powertrain management system to identify the component failure modes (e.g., torque-request signal faults, deceleration logic errors) behind the unintended acceleration and vibration during deceleration, then implement a redundant powertrain-control architecture (dual torque-request channels with cross-monitoring and fail-safe torque limiting) so a single-point fault cannot command spontaneous acceleration on lift-off.
architecture.expected_effect: The optimized powertrain architecture lowers the failure frequency and unavailability of the unintended-acceleration hazard, so the vehicle decelerates smoothly with no spontaneous acceleration or vibration when approaching a stop.
architecture.falsification_test: Instrument the vehicle to log throttle position, motor/torque request, and wheel speed; inject single-point faults (open/short circuits, stale torque-request values, task timing failures) into the torque path during deceleration-to-stop maneuvers; if any injected fault produces spontaneous acceleration or 3-second vibration bursts, the redundant design fails and must be revised.
